abstract: Plant-derived extracellular vesicles (PEVs) have been regarded as a superior source for nanomedicine and drug delivery systems. Nevertheless, their clinical translation is hindered by the lack of clarity and even contradiction in their biomedical applications. Herein, we conducted a comprehensive compositional analysis of four commonly used PEVs to fully understand their functional lipid contents and assess their potential therapeutic applications. The lipidomic analysis revealed the presence of cytotoxic gingerols and shogaols in ginger-derived EVs (GEVs). Subsequent in vitro and in vivo investigations substantiated the remarkable tumor cell inhibitory and tumor growth suppression efficacy of GEVs. The transcriptomic analysis indicated that GEVs regulate the cell cycle and p53 signaling pathways, thereby inducing cancer cell apoptosis. The supplementary proteomic analysis suggested the potential protein markers in PEV research. These findings highlight the value of multi-omics analyses in elucidating the potential therapeutic effects of PEVs and in advancing the development of PEV-based therapies.

Materials and methods
4.1
Isolation of plant-derived EVs (PEVs)
Grapefruit (Genus,
Citrus
; Family, Rutaceae; Order, Sapindales; Class, Magnoliopsida), ginger (Genus,
Zingiber
; Family, Zingiberaceae; Order, Zingiberales; Class, Liliopsida), lemon (Genus,
Citrus
; Family, Rutaceae; Order, Sapindales; Class, Magnoliopsida) and grape (Genus,
Vitis
; Family, Vitaceae; Order, Vitales; Class, Magnoliopsida) were obtained at local agricultural market. Grapefruit, ginger, lemons, and grapes were thoroughly washed with deionized water and then peeled. The obtained pulp was plated into a juicer and homogenized in PBS (Labgic Technology Co., Ltd) to get juice. Afterwards, the obtained juice was differentially centrifuged at 1000 g for 10 min, 3000 g for 30 min, and 10000 g for 1 h. The supernatant was collected and then ultracentrifuged at 100,000 g for 2 h (Beckman Optima MAX-XP). The pellet was resuspended in PBS buffer and the suspension was filtered using 0.22 μm membrane filters. The obtained PEVs were then stored at −80 °C for further use.
4.2
Characterization of PEVs
The morphology of obtained PEVs was analyzed using transmission electron microscopy TEM (Thermo Fisher Talos L120C) at an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. The concentration and size distribution of PEVs were determined using a nanoparticle tracking analyzer (Malvern NanoSight NS300). Data was shown as mean ± standard deviation (SD) (n = 3). The zeta potentials of PEVs were measured via dynamic light scattering (DLS) using a particle analyzer (Brookhaven Instruments NanoBrook Omni).
4.3
Extraction of lipid metabolites
The isolated PEVs were thawed on ice. Subsequently, 20 μL of each type of PEV sample was mixed with 240 μL of precooled lipid extraction solution (isopropyl alcohol: acetonitrile: H
2
O = 2:1:1), and then vortexed thoroughly for 1 min. The mixture solutions were then incubated at room temperature for 10 min, and then stored at −20 °C overnight. Then, the mixture solutions were subjected to centrifugation at 4000
g
for 20 min, after which the supernatant solutions were collected and stored at −80 °C in preparation for further LC-MS analysis.
4.4
LC-MS analysis
The isolated lipid metabolites derived from four types of PEVs were analyzed by the LC-MS system. The chromatographic separations were conducted using an UPLC system (ACQUITY, Waters Corporation). A Kinetex UPLC C18 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 100A, Phenomenex) was used for reversed phase separation. The temperature of the column oven was set at 55 °C. The flow rate was 1 mL/min. The mobile phase was composed of two solvents, A and B. Solvent A was a solution of acetonitrile and water in a 6:4 ratio, with the addition of 0.1 % formic acid. Solvent B was an isopropyl alcohol and acetonitrile solution in a 9:1 ratio, with the addition of 0.1 % formic acid. The gradient elution conditions were established as follows: 0–0.4 min, 30 % B; 0.4–1 min, 30 %–45 % B; 1–3 min, 45 %–60 % B; 3.5–5 min, 60 %–75 % B; 5–7 min, 75 %–90 % B; 7–8.5 min, 90 %–100 % B; 8.5–8.6 min, 100 % B; 8.6–8.61 min, 100 %–30 % B; 8.61–10 min, 30 % B. A high-resolution tandem mass spectrometer (TripleTOF6600, SCIEX) was employed to detect the lipid contents eluted from the column. The same methodology was also applied to detect shogaols and gingerols in GEV-derived lipids. The standard samples of 6,8,10-gingerol and 6, 8, 10-shogaol were purchased from MedChemExpress (MCE).
The Quadrupole Time-of-Flight (Q-TOF) was conducted in both positive and negative ion modes. The curtain gas was set at 30 PSI, the ion source gas 1 was set at 60 PSI, the ion source gas 2 was set at 60 PSI, and the interface heater temperature was set at 650°. In the case of the positive ion mode, the Ionspray voltage was set at 5000 V, while in the negative ion mode, the Ionspray voltage was set at −4500 V. The mass spectrometry data were acquired in IDA mode. The TOF mass range was determined to be between 60 and 1200 Da. The survey scans were acquired in 150 ms, and as many as 12 product ion scans were collected if the threshold of 100 counts/s was exceeded and the charge state was 1+. The total cycle time was fixed at 0.56 s. Four time bins were summed for each scan at a pulser frequency value of 11 kHz through the monitoring of the 40 GHz multichannel TDC detector with four-anode/channel detection. A dynamic exclusion setting of 4 s was implemented. During the acquisition process, the mass accuracy was calibrated every 20 samples. Furthermore, in order to assess the reliability of the LC-MS throughout the entire acquisition process, a quality control (QC) sample was prepared by mixing 10 μL of each lipid extraction type and acquired after every 10 samples.
4.5
Cell culture
B16F10 and luciferase-producing B16F10 (B16F10-luc) melanoma cell lines were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, USA). These two types of cells were respectively cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Gibco) supplemented with 10 % Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS, Gibco), 100 U/mL of penicillin (Gibco), and 100 μg/mL of streptomycin (Gibco). The cells were incubated under 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5 % CO
2
and routinely passaged with a standard trypsin (Gibco)-based method when cell density reached about 90 %. The hypoxic environment for cell culture was maintained via introduction of gas mixture of N
2
(94 %), CO
2
(5 % CO
2
), and O
2
(1 %).

4

9

Cell proliferation
B16F10 cells were pretreated with GEVs (0, 1, 5, 10 × 10
9
/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C and then seeded into 6-well plates (1 × 10
3

4.8
Colony formation assay
B16F10 cells were pretreated with GEVs (0, 1, 5, 10 × 10
9
/mL) for 24 h. The pretreated cells were then seeded into 6-well plates (200 cells/well) and were continuously cultured at 37 °C for 7 days with culture medium replacement every two days. Colony growth was monitored during the colony formation phase. On day 7, the cells were gently washed with PBS for three times and then fixed with 4 % of PFA (Labgic Technology Co., Ltd) for 20 min at 37 °C. After three washes with PBS, the cells were stained with crystal violet (0.5 % w/v, ECOTOP) for 30 min at room temperature. The plates were then washed with water under shaking until the stain was removed. The stained colonies were then photographed with camera and counted for analysis.
4.9
Live dead cell assay
B16F10 cells were seeded into a 6-well plate at a density of 3 × 10
5
cells/well, and incubated overnight at 37 °C. The cells were then incubated with GEVs (0, 1, 5, and 10 × 10
9
/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C. The treated cells were then washed with PBS for three times, and subsequently stained with Calcein-AM (2 μM, Beyotime Biotechnology) and PI (5 μM, Beyotime Biotechnology) for 30 min at 37 °C. The cell images were immediately evaluated using a fluorescence microscope (Thermo Scientific EVOS M5000). Live cells were stained by Calcein-AM (Excitation: 488 nm; emission: 517 nm) and dead cells were stained by PI (Excitation: 561 nm; emission: 617 nm), separately.
4.10
Cell apoptosis assay
The therapeutic effect of GEVs on tumor cell apoptosis was determined via an annexin V-FITC/PI cell apoptosis assay and TUNEL assay. For the annexin V-FITC/PI cell apoptosis assay, B16F10 cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 3 × 10
5
cells/well, and incubated overnight at 37 °C. The cells were then incubated with GEVs (0, 1, 5, and 10 × 10
9
/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C. The treated cells were then washed with PBS, centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min, and resuspended in 500 μL 1 × binding buffer. The cells were then stained with annexin V-FITC (5 μL, BestBio) and PI (5 μL, BestBio) for 15 min in the dark. After staining, the stained cells were analyzed using a flow cytometer (Agilent NovoCyte Quamteon) and the data was analyzed. For the TUNEL assay, B16F10 cells were seeded in 35-mm glass-bottomed dishes at a density of 1 × 10
5
cells/well, and incubated overnight at 37 °C. The cells were then incubated with GEVs (0, and 5 × 10
9
/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C. After that, the cells were subjected to TUNEL staining using the One-step TUNEL In Situ Apoptosis Kit (Green, Elab Fluor® 488) (Elabscience), in accordance with the instructions provided. After that, the cells were washed with PBS and stained by DAPI (5 μg/mL, Beyotime Biotechnology) for 20 min. After washing with PBS for three times, the cells were subjected to CLSM analysis using a confocal microscope (LSM900, Zeiss). The excitation and emission wavelengths for TUNEL-positive cells are 488 nm and 519 nm, respectively. The excitation and emission wavelengths for DAPI are 405 nm and 461 nm, respectively.
4.11
Preparation and characterization of GEV-iRGDs
DSPE-PEG-iRGD (Ruixi Biological Technology Co) solution was added into GEV solution at a ratio of 20000:1. After that, the mixture was subjected to oscillation for 4 h at 4 °C. After that, the GEV-iRGDs were washed with PBS using a 10 kDa ultrafiltration centrifuge tube (Merck millipore). The size distribution and zeta potentials of GEV-iRGD were measured via DLS using a particle analyzer (Brookhaven Instruments NanoBrook Omni). DSPE-PEG-iRGD-FITC (Tanshtech Co., Ltd) was added into GEV solution for reaction for 4 h at 4 °C, and then washed three times with PBS using a 10 kDa ultrafiltration centrifuge tube to get DSPE-PEG-iRGD-FITC-labelled GEVs. Subsequently, the GEVs and DSPE-PEG-iRGD-FITC-treated GEVs were subjected to flow cytometry analysis to ascertain the modification of iRGD on the GEVs.
4.12
Cellular uptake assay
The cellular uptake of GEVs and GEV-iRGDs was determined via flow cytometry and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM). DSPE-PEG-FITC (Ruixi Biological Technology Co) was added into GEV solution for reaction for 4 h at 4 °C, and then washed with PBS using a 10 kDa ultrafiltration centrifuge tube to get FITC-labelled GEVs. For flow cytometry, B16F10 cells were seeded in 12-well plates (Labgic Technology Co., Ltd) at a density of 1 × 10
5
cells/well, and incubated overnight at 37 °C. The cells were then incubated with FITC-labelled GEVs and GEV-iRGDs (10
7
, 10
8
/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C. After that, the cells were collected and analyzed using a flow cytometer (Agilent NovoCyte Quamteon) and the data was analyzed. For CLSM, B16F10 cells were seeded in 35-mm glass-bottomed dishes at a density of 1 × 10
5
cells/well, and incubated overnight at 37 °C. The cells were then incubated with FITC-labelled GEVs and GEV-iRGDs (10
7
, 10
8
/mL) for 24 h at 37 °C. After that, the cells were washed with PBS and stained by DAPI (5 μg/mL, Beyotime Biotechnology) for 20 min. After washing with PBS for three times, the cells were subjected to CLSM analysis using a confocal microscope (LSM900, Zeiss). The excitation and emission wavelengths for FITC-positive cells are 488 nm and 517 nm, respectively. The excitation and emission wavelengths for DAPI are 405 nm and 461 nm, respectively.
4.13
In vivo biodistribution
Female C57BL/6J mice (4 weeks, about 20 g) were bought from Huachuang Sino PharmaTech Co., Ltd. and housed in the Laboratory Animal Research Unit (LARU) at the Tenth Affiliated Hospital of Southern Medical University under pathogen-free condition. First, the B16F10 melanoma mouse model was established by subcutaneous injection of 1 × 10
6
B16F10 cells (in 100 μL PBS) into the left flank of each mouse. After 7 d, the mice were randomly divided into two groups. Each mouse received an intravenous injection of either DSPE-PEG-Cy5-labelled GEVs or GEV-iRGDs (in 100 μL PBS) at a concentration of 1 × 10
9
GEVs or GEV-iRGDs per mouse. The mice were then sacrificed at 4 h, 24 h, and 72 h post injection and major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidneys, and tumor) were collected and imaged via IVIS Spectrum Imaging System (PerkinElmer IVIS Spectrum). The excitation and emission wavelengths are 640 nm and 700 nm, respectively, with an excitation time of 30 s. The data was analyzed using the Living Image Software. To study the distribution of GEVs and GEV-iRGDs, the collected livers and tumors were fixed in 4 % PFA, followed by dehydration in 30 % sucrose (Saiguo Biotech Co., LTD) overnight. These tissues were then embedded in optimum cutting temperature compound (OCT, Sakura) for frozen sectioning. The sections were incubated with DAPI (5 μg/mL, Beyotime Biotechnology) for 5 min to counterstain cell nuclei. The tissue sections were subjected to CLSM analysis using a confocal microscope (LSM900, Zeiss). The excitation and emission wavelengths for Cy5 are 640 nm and 670 nm, respectively. The excitation and emission wavelengths for DAPI are 405 nm and 461 nm, respectively.
4.14
In vivo anti-tumor therapy
B16F10 melanoma mouse model was established by subcutaneous injection of 1 × 10
6
B16F10 cells (in 100 μL PBS) into the left flank of each mouse. When the tumor volume reached about 60 mm
3
, the mice were randomly divided into three groups (n = 6): (1) Control (Ctrl) group with mice received intravenous injection of 100 μL PBS; (2) GEVs group with mice received intravenous injection of GEVs (2 × 10
10
in 100 μL PBS); and (3) GEV-iRGDs group with mice received intravenous injection of GEV-iRGDs (2 × 10
10
in 100 μL PBS), respectively. The formulations were administered every other day for three treatments total. The tumor volume and mouse weight were recorded every other day during the treatment duration. The tumor volume was calculated in accordance with following formula:
V
(volume) = length × width
2
/2. At day 14, all the mice were sacrificed by CO
2
exposure and dissected. Major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidneys, and tumor) and blood samples were collected for analysis.
4.15
H&E staining, TUNEL staining, and immunohistochemistry (IHC)
For histological studies, the harvested major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidneys, and tumor) were fixed with 4 % of PFA, and then dissected into 5-μm sections. After that, the tissue sections were stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin solution (Labgic Technology Co., Ltd) to access the histological changes. The photographs of all the tissue sections were observed using a Research Slide Scanner (Olympus SlideView VS200). For terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) staining, the tumor sections were fixed with 4 % of PFA and then washed with PBS for 20 min. Afterwards, the tumor sections were stained with TUNEL reaction solution (100 μL, Elabscience) for 1 h at room temperature. After washing with PBS, the tumor sections were stained with DAPI for 30 min and then subjected to CLSM analysis using a confocal microscope (Zeiss LSM900). Immunohistochemistry was employed to determine the cell proliferation in tumor tissues. Tumor sections were blocked with 5 % milk for 1 h at room temperature, washed, and incubated with primary antibody against Ki-67 (1:500,
GB121141
, Servicebio) at 4 °C overnight. After washing, tumor sections were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (1:200, GB23301, Servicebio) for 1 h. The histological photographs of tumor tissues were observed under a Research Slide Scanner (Olympus SlideView VS200).
4.16
Blood routine tests and biochemical analysis
The blood samples from each group were collected subjected to routine blood tests to determine the hematological parameters. In addition, the blood samples were allowed to clot at room temperature. The blood samples were then centrifuged at 2000 g for 20 min and the supernatant serum were transferred into new tubes. Afterwards, the serum samples were subjected to biochemical analysis to evaluate biochemistry parameters, including blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine (CR), uric acid (UA), serum alanine transaminase (ALT), and serum aspartate transaminase (AST).
4.17
RNA sequencing assay
Total RNA sample was extracted from GEV-pretreated B16F10 cells using Trizol reagent (Thermo Fisher) under the manufacturer's instructions. The RNA samples were further subjected to RNA quantification, purification, cDNA library synthesis, and RNA sequencing at LC-BIO Technologies (Hangzhou, China). The RNA sequencing data was then analyzed in R 3.6.3.
4.18
Quantitative real-time PCR
Total RNA was isolated from B16F10 cells pretreated with GEVs (0, 5 × 10
9
/mL) using a Eastep® Super Total RNA Extraction Kit (Promega Corporation) under the manufacturer's instructions. RNA concentration was then determined using a microdrop. For each group, 1 μg RNA was subjected to reverse transcription for cDNA synthesis using TransScript First-Strand Synthesis SuperMix Kit (Takara). After that, quantitative real-time PCR was conducted using TransStart Tip Green qPCR SuperMix (Takara) on a digital PCR system (ABI QuantStudio 5), and the data was subsequently analyzed using QuantStudio design & analysis software. Primer sequences used in this study was shown in
Supplementary Table 1
.
4.19
Statistical analysis
All experiments were performed at least in triplicate independently for each group, and the statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism Software (version 8). The results were shown as mean ± SD. Two-tailed, unpaired Student's
t
-test was applied for difference analysis of two groups. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and two-way ANOVA were applied for difference analysis for multiple groups.
p
< 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Introduction
At present, extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from mammalian sources are regarded as natural therapeutics and drug delivery systems for next-generation of nanomedicine, with considerable potential for application across numerous biomedical fields [
[1]
,
[2]
,
[3]
]. However, their clinical translation suffers from several obstacles, particularly low yield and lack of large-scale manufacturing techniques [
[4]
,
[5]
,
[6]
,
[7]
]. Recently, plant-derived EVs (PEVs) have been subjected to investigation as a potential sustainable alternative for the scale-up isolation of therapeutic EVs [
8
,
9
]. This can be traced back to 1967, when scientists first observed and discovered the existence of extracellular vesicles in carrot cell cultures [
10
]. However, until the past two decades, the isolation, characterization, and applications of PEVs have been illuminated by emerging research [
11
].
PEVs have been demonstrated to share similar physicochemical properties with those of mammalian-derived EVs, including morphology, size distribution, surface charge, etc. Of note, PEVs also contain biomolecules, including proteins, lipids, and other metabolites [
12
]. Therefore, PEVs are considered a novel type of natural nanomedicine with therapeutic effects inherited from their original source. In addition, PEVs are believed to be safe and biocompatible for human consumption, as they are isolated from edible and medicinal plants [
13
]. Consequently, recent studies have concentrated on the therapeutic potential of PEVs in the treatment of a range of diseases, especially anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative stress, and anti-cancer applications [
[14]
,
[15]
,
[16]
]. Furthermore, PEVs represent a superior alternative to synthetic nanoparticles and mammalian-derived EVs as a drug delivery system in consideration of immunogenicity, adverse reactions, biostability, and scalability [
[17]
,
[18]
,
[19]
].
Notwithstanding the notable successes in biomedical applications of PEVs, their clinical translation remains severely constrained by the confusing rigor of PEV research in its nascent stages. Thus far, PEVs isolated from the same source have been used for different biomedical applications. For example, studies have shown that lemon-derived EVs (LEVs) have anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory effects [
20
,
21
]. Conversely, other studies have shown that LEVs induce cell apoptosis and inhibit tumor growth via amelioration of ROS levels or TRAIL stimulation [
22
,
23
]. These studies appear to be in contradiction with one another. In addition, PEVs derived from grapefruit, ginger and
Aloe vera
peels have been demonstrated to be effective in anti-oxidant biomedical applications [
14
,
24
,
25
]. However, it is notable that these studies have not yet compared the efficacy of the PEVs, nor have they optimized the PEVs for anti-oxidant utilization.
A comprehensive understanding of the composition of PEVs is essential for fully elucidating and further assessing their therapeutic potential, as the substances within them determine their functions. Recent studies have employed high-throughput sequencing techniques to identify a diverse array of small RNA species within PEVs, thereby advancing our knowledge of the RNA compositions and potential effects of PEVs [
[26]
,
[27]
,
[28]
,
[29]
]. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of PEVs has not yet been fully realized, in part due to a lack of detailed investigation into the major functional lipid component of PEVs [
[30]
,
[31]
,
[32]
]. Furthermore, the absence of suitable and reliable markers for PEVs impedes their isolation, classification, and detailed analysis [
9
,
33
]. Consequently, compositional lipidomic and proteomic analyses of PEVs are essential to enhance our understanding of their potential biological and pharmacological effects and to identify the long-awaited PEV markers, as well as to facilitate the prediction and optimization of their potential therapeutic applications [
34
].
In this study, we employed a multi-omics approach to perform a systematic compositional analysis of PEVs. The objective was to identify the lipid and protein contents and provide guidance for their downstream biomedical applications (
Fig. 1
). The PEVs were isolated and characterized from grapefruit (GFEVs), ginger (GEVs), lemon (LEVs), and grape (GPEVs), which are four of the most commonly used plant sources. The lipidomic analysis revealed the presence of cytotoxic gingerol and shogaol compounds in GEVs (
Fig. 1
a). The present study provided detailed evidence of the anti-proliferative and apoptotic properties of GEVs against cancer cells. It was of note that the modification of GEVs with tumor-targeting iRGD promoted their uptake in cancer cells and accumulation in tumor tissues, leading to a remarkable efficacy in suppressing tumors (
Fig. 1
b). The quantitative proteomic analysis indicated the existence of potential protein markers for further investigation in PEV research. These findings indicate the necessity of a multi-omics approach to enhance our comprehension of the potential pharmacological impact of PEVs and facilitate the development of innovative PEV-based therapeutic agents.

Results
2.1
Preparation and characterization of PEVs
In order to conduct a systematic compositional analysis of PEVs, we selected four types of edible plants, including grapefruit, ginger, lemon, and grape, that were commonly used for PEV isolation [
35
]. Four types of PEVs were isolated via the differential centrifugation technique, including grapefruit-derived EVs (GFEVs), ginger-derived EVs (GEVs), lemon-derived EVs (LEVs), and grape-derived EVs (GPEVs) (
Fig. 2
a). As illustrated in the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images, the four types of PEVs exhibited a typical cup-like shape of EVs, though the sizes varied among them (
Fig. 2
b). Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) revealed the sizes of four types of PEVs, with the peak value centered at 156 nm for GFEVs, 197 nm for GEVs, 107 nm for LEVs, and 191 nm for GPEVs (
Fig. 2
c). In addition, the zeta potentials were determined to be −24.90 ± 2.88 mV for GFEVs, −39.61 ± 1.93 mV for GEVs, −23.57 ± 2.06 mV for LEVs, and −25.25 ± 2.64 mV for GPEVs (
Fig. 2
d). The data presented herein demonstrate the successful isolation of PEVs.

Scale bar, 100 nm. (c) Size distribution of GFEVs, GEVs, LEVs, and GPEVs determined by nanoparticle tracking analysis. (d) Zeta potential values of GFEVs, GEVs, LEVs, and GPEVs (n = 3). Data are mean ± SD.

2.2
Comparative lipidomic analyses of PEVs
Subsequently, an investigation and comparative analysis of the lipid compositions of four types of PEVs was conducted utilizing a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) system. The principal component analysis (PCA) revealed a distinct clustering for the triplicates of each type of PEVs. Additionally, there was a high degree of similarity between the GFEV and LEV groups, with a clear separation from the other groups (
Fig. 3
a). The high degree of similarity between the lipids derived from GFEVs and LEVs may be attributed to the close evolutionary relationship between grapefruit and lemon, as both belong to the
Citrus
genus [
36
]. Collectively, a total of 16623, 49139, 23314, and 10832 molecules were detected from GFEVs, GEVs, LEVs, and GPEVs, respectively (
Fig. S1
). Of these, 982 (5.91 %), 1322 (2.69 %), 1174 (5.04 %), and 796 (7.35 %) lipid species were identified, respectively (
Fig. 3
b). To compare lipids that differed among the four types of PEVs, we performed hierarchical clustering analysis based on the relative abundance of differentially detected lipids. The hierarchical clustering heatmap demonstrated a notable disparity in the abundance of these lipids between the four distinct types of PEVs (
Fig. 3
c). The quantitative analysis separately detected six lipid categories, including glycerolipids, sphingolipids, sterol lipids, fatty acyls, glycerophospholipids, and prenol lipids. The relative proportion of these lipid categories varied in different PEVs (
Fig. 3
d). As shown, GFEVs contained highest level of glycerophospholipids (50.05 %), while GEVs (46.23 %), LEVs (53.77 %), and GPEVs (47.97 %) contains highest level of glycerolipids. Correspondingly, the relative ratios of glycerophospholipids decreased in GEVs (5.25 %), LEVs (23.24 %), and GPEVs (27.14 %). Of special note, significantly lower ratio of glycerophospholipids and significantly higher ratio of fatty acyls were identified in GEVs. The proportions of sterol lipids (∼10 %), and prenol lipids (<0.2 %) remained stable in four types of PEVs. Assessing the relative abundance of lipid classes of these categories revealed their varied intensity among different PEVs (
Fig. S2a
). For example, fatty acids (FA) in GEVs accounted for about 40-fold than that in GPEVs and 5.6-fold than that in GFEVs, though FA accounted for more than 80 % of total fatty acyls in all four types of PEVs. The number and relative proportion of the top 10 lipid classes in each type of PEVs were shown (
Fig. 3
e and
Fig. S2b
). The Venn diagram revealed 465 lipid species were commonly identified in four types of PEVs, and 29, 400, 87, and 40 unique lipid species were exclusively detected in GFEVs, GEVs, LEVs, and GPEVs, respectively (
Fig. 3
f).

Quantitative proteomic analysis and potential markers of PEVs
It has been suggested that the most pressing need in this novel field is the identification of a set of suitable and reliable protein markers for PEVs [
33
]. In order to identify the potential markers for PEVs, we further performed a quantitative proteomic analysis. We isolated total proteins from four types of PEVs using radio immunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer, and the protein concentrations were subsequently measured. An average of 31.38, 64.89, 11.19, and 8.96 μg total proteins was found to be extracted from 10
10
GFEVs, GEVs, LEVs, and GPEVs, respectively (
Fig. S20a
). Subsequently, we conducted 4D-label-free proteomic analysis using an HPLC system to determine the protein content in isolated PEVs. The number of proteins identified in each type of PEV is shown (
Fig. S20b
). Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated a distinct clustering of the triplicates within each type of PEVs, indicating the reliability of the isolation technique (
Fig. S20c
). In addition, the PCA revealed a high degree of similarity in the proteomic profiles between the GFEV group and the LEV group, with a clear cluster separation evident from and among the other two groups. The Venn diagram demonstrated that a total of 1238 proteins were commonly detected in four types of PEVs, whereas 386, 1355, 250, and 379 unique proteins were exclusively expressed in GFEVs, GEVs, LEVs, and GPEVs, respectively (
Fig. S20d
). The generated intensity heatmap permitted the observation of subtype-specific protein clusters in comparisons between different samples (
Fig. S20e
). Six largest clusters (containing 932, 389, 2165, 551, 612, and 933 protein groups) with varied patterns in relative protein intensity across different sources were selected for further analysis and shown (
Fig. S20f
). In addition, cellular component analyses indicate that the proteins identified in PEVs originate from various cellular components (
Fig. S20g
). The three most prevalent sources of proteins identified in PEVs are the cytoplasm, cell membrane, and nucleus. These data suggested the complexity of PEVs and the contribution of different subcellular compartments with different lipid membranes to the PEV content during the preparation and isolation process, which is consistent with a previous report [
45
].
We conducted a proteomic analysis and compared the identified proteins with those frequently observed in mammalian-derived EVs. As illustrated, twenty-four of the top 100 most prevalent EV proteins listed in the Vesiclepedia databases were successfully identified in our proteomics analyses (
Fig. S20h
). The relative intensity of each protein group is presented in the form of a heatmap. In addition to the aforementioned considerations, the level of potential proteins in the PEVs is also of importance. Consequently, an analysis and comparison of the top 200 proteins in each type of PEVs was conducted, resulting in the identification of 16 proteins that were commonly expressed (
Fig. S20i
). The heatmap illustrates the varying intensities of the identified proteins (
Fig. S20j
). Furthermore, four proteins, including heat shock protein 70 (V4UFD6), ubiquitin-60S ribosomal protein L40 (A0A438JSE9), actin (F6HJM9), and elongation factor 1-alpha (V4SBI0), are among the top 100 proteins in each type of PEVs. By integrating the two perspectives, we were able to identify three proteins with high expression levels in PEVs and corresponding to the commonly identified proteins in mammalian-derived EVs, namely heat shock protein 70, actin, and elongation factor 1-alpha (
Fig. S21
). This suggests that these proteins may serve as specific markers for PEV research. Unfortunately, we were unable to further test this hypothesis at this time due to the unavailability of commercial antibodies against the aforementioned putative PEV marker candidates. The prospective development of commercial antibodies directed against plant proteins would simplify the isolation and characterization of PEVs, which would be advantageous for the quality control of these materials.
3
Discussion and conclusion
Plant-derived extracellular vesicles (PEVs), which displayed inherent therapeutic efficacy and could be subjected to scale-up isolation, are considered a sustainable and reliable source of natural nanomedicine and drug delivery nanoplatforms [
46
,
47
]. Although the biomedical applications of PEVs are undoubtedly exciting, they are also confusing and sometimes contradictory. The complex and multifaceted nature of PEV research, particularly with regard to their potential applications, necessitates a comprehensive investigation into the functional substances and underlying molecular mechanisms of their biological activities. This would facilitate the comparation and optimization of PEVs in the context of specific disease therapeutic applications [
17
,
48
,
49
]. We propose that a comprehensive analysis of the molecular composition of PEVs, in particular the major functional lipid contents, could enhance our understanding of their intrinsic therapeutic potential and facilitate the prediction and guidance of the development and standardization of treatment methodologies for various diseases using different PEVs.
In this study, we initially isolated PEVs from four commonly used edible plants, including grapefruit (GFEVs), ginger (GEVs), lemon (LEVs), and grape (GPEVs). TEM imaging, NTA, and DLS characterizations confirmed the typical morphology, size distribution and surface potential of the obtained PEVs, which are consistent with those of mammalian-derived EVs. The comparative analysis of the lipid contents revealed notable differences in the lipid number and abundance between the four types of PEVs, with GEVs from the other three exhibiting particularly distinct characteristics. It is noteworthy that the presence of 6-shogaol, 8-shogaol, and 10-shogaol was identified in GEVs, which exhibited notable cytotoxicity. Consequently, we confirmed the concentration-dependent cytotoxicity of GEVs and conducted a detailed analysis of their anti-proliferative and cell apoptosis induction effects against cancer cells. Prior research has demonstrated the anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidant properties of GEVs and their application in the treatment of different diseases [
14
,
50
]. Conversely, our demonstration of the comparative lipidomic analyses revealed the anti-cancer potential of the GEV-based therapeutics.
The GEVs were modified with tumor-targeting iRGD, and enhanced cellular uptake
in vitro
and tumor accumulation
in vivo
of GEVs after iRGD modification was observed, indicating the remarkable tumor-targeting property of GEV-iRGDs. Moreover, GEV-iRGDs demonstrated superior efficacy in suppressing tumors compared to GEVs, likely due to their tumor-targeting and accumulation properties. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that GEV treatment primarily influenced cell cycle and p53 signaling pathways, which are apoptosis-related pathways, ultimately leading to cancer cell death and tumor inhibition.
The protein markers for PEVs are not yet available due to the relative novelty of this research area and the relatively limited number of PEV proteomics analyses. Nevertheless, the requirement of suitable and reliable protein markers for PEVs is urgent due to their important roles in determining the yield and purity of PEVs and further developing and standardizing PEV-based therapeutics [
33
]. Accordingly, we also performed a quantitative proteomic analysis to find the potential markers of PEVs. The analysis revealed the diverse protein composition, relative abundance, and cellular component sources. By considering the EV markers in mammalian-derived EVs and the protein levels in PEVs, we identified heat shock protein 70, actin, and elongation factor 1-alpha as potential markers for PEV research. The future development of commercial antibodies will facilitate the verification of PEV markers identified in this study.
Overall, we performed systematic composition analyses subsequent utilization of PEVs. The lipidomic analysis prompted us to investigate the proof-of-concept anti-cancer therapy using GEVs, demonstrating the significance of advanced multi-omics techniques in the prediction and guidance of their potential biomedical applications. Furthermore, proteomic analyses may facilitate the identification of specific markers on PEVs that assist in their classification and isolation. We envision that our study will facilitate the advancement of rigorous and standardized research and therapeutic development based on PEVs.

4.1
Isolation of plant-derived EVs (PEVs)
Grapefruit (Genus,
Citrus
; Family, Rutaceae; Order, Sapindales; Class, Magnoliopsida), ginger (Genus,
Zingiber
; Family, Zingiberaceae; Order, Zingiberales; Class, Liliopsida), lemon (Genus,
Citrus
; Family, Rutaceae; Order, Sapindales; Class, Magnoliopsida) and grape (Genus,
Vitis
; Family, Vitaceae; Order, Vitales; Class, Magnoliopsida) were obtained at local agricultural market. Grapefruit, ginger, lemons, and grapes were thoroughly washed with deionized water and then peeled. The obtained pulp was plated into a juicer and homogenized in PBS (Labgic Technology Co., Ltd) to get juice. Afterwards, the obtained juice was differentially centrifuged at 1000 g for 10 min, 3000 g for 30 min, and 10000 g for 1 h. The supernatant was collected and then ultracentrifuged at 100,000 g for 2 h (Beckman Optima MAX-XP). The pellet was resuspended in PBS buffer and the suspension was filtered using 0.22 μm membrane filters. The obtained PEVs were then stored at −80 °C for further use.
4.2
Characterization of PEVs
The morphology of obtained PEVs was analyzed using transmission electron microscopy TEM (Thermo Fisher Talos L120C) at an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. The concentration and size distribution of PEVs were determined using a nanoparticle tracking analyzer (Malvern NanoSight NS300). Data was shown as mean ± standard deviation (SD) (n = 3). The zeta potentials of PEVs were measured via dynamic light scattering (DLS) using a particle analyzer (Brookhaven Instruments NanoBrook Omni).
4.3
Extraction of lipid metabolites
The isolated PEVs were thawed on ice. Subsequently, 20 μL of each type of PEV sample was mixed with 240 μL of precooled lipid extraction solution (isopropyl alcohol: acetonitrile: H
2
O = 2:1:1), and then vortexed thoroughly for 1 min. The mixture solutions were then incubated at room temperature for 10 min, and then stored at −20 °C overnight. Then, the mixture solutions were subjected to centrifugation at 4000
g
for 20 min, after which the supernatant solutions were collected and stored at −80 °C in preparation for further LC-MS analysis.
4.4
LC-MS analysis
The isolated lipid metabolites derived from four types of PEVs were analyzed by the LC-MS system. The chromatographic separations were conducted using an UPLC system (ACQUITY, Waters Corporation). A Kinetex UPLC C18 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 100A, Phenomenex) was used for reversed phase separation. The temperature of the column oven was set at 55 °C. The flow rate was 1 mL/min. The mobile phase was composed of two solvents, A and B. Solvent A was a solution of acetonitrile and water in a 6:4 ratio, with the addition of 0.1 % formic acid. Solvent B was an isopropyl alcohol and acetonitrile solution in a 9:1 ratio, with the addition of 0.1 % formic acid. The gradient elution conditions were established as follows: 0–0.4 min, 30 % B; 0.4–1 min, 30 %–45 % B; 1–3 min, 45 %–60 % B; 3.5–5 min, 60 %–75 % B; 5–7 min, 75 %–90 % B; 7–8.5 min, 90 %–100 % B; 8.5–8.6 min, 100 % B; 8.6–8.61 min, 100 %–30 % B; 8.61–10 min, 30 % B. A high-resolution tandem mass spectrometer (TripleTOF6600, SCIEX) was employed to detect the lipid contents eluted from the column. The same methodology was also applied to detect shogaols and gingerols in GEV-derived lipids. The standard samples of 6,8,10-gingerol and 6, 8, 10-shogaol were purchased from MedChemExpress (MCE).
The Quadrupole Time-of-Flight (Q-TOF) was conducted in both positive and negative ion modes. The curtain gas was set at 30 PSI, the ion source gas 1 was set at 60 PSI, the ion source gas 2 was set at 60 PSI, and the interface heater temperature was set at 650°. In the case of the positive ion mode, the Ionspray voltage was set at 5000 V, while in the negative ion mode, the Ionspray voltage was set at −4500 V. The mass spectrometry data were acquired in IDA mode. The TOF mass range was determined to be between 60 and 1200 Da. The survey scans were acquired in 150 ms, and as many as 12 product ion scans were collected if the threshold of 100 counts/s was exceeded and the charge state was 1+. The total cycle time was fixed at 0.56 s. Four time bins were summed for each scan at a pulser frequency value of 11 kHz through the monitoring of the 40 GHz multichannel TDC detector with four-anode/channel detection. A dynamic exclusion setting of 4 s was implemented. During the acquisition process, the mass accuracy was calibrated every 20 samples. Furthermore, in order to assess the reliability of the LC-MS throughout the entire acquisition process, a quality control (QC) sample was prepared by mixing 10 μL of each lipid extraction type and acquired after every 10 samples.
